title: Solomon's Kingdom at Its Height
overview: After finishing the temple and his palace, Solomon builds towns, organizes labor and worship, and sends ships abroad for gold.

parts.label: Building towns and forts (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: After twenty years of building, Solomon strengthened his kingdom with fortified towns, supply centers and bases for his chariots, reaching as far as Tadmor in the Syrian desert, later known as Palmyra. First Kings says Solomon gave towns to Hiram, the king of Tyre, while this verse says Hiram gave towns to Solomon, and how the two accounts fit together is unclear.

parts.label: Forced labor and officers (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Descendants of the peoples who lived in the land before Israel were made into a permanent forced labor force, while Israelites served as soldiers and officials. This was labor forced on people because of their ancestry, and the writer reports it plainly; the number of supervisors also differs from First Kings, likely through a copying error.

parts.label: A separate palace for his wife (v. 11)
parts.note: Solomon moved his Egyptian wife, Pharaoh's daughter, out of the City of David into a palace built for her, saying David's palace was no place for her because places the ark, the sacred chest seen as marking God's presence, had entered were holy. Interpreters usually take this to mean that a foreign queen with her own gods and household was felt to be out of place so near such holy ground.

parts.label: Worship put in order (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: Solomon kept the schedule of offerings from the law of Moses, daily, weekly, monthly and at three yearly festivals, and arranged priests, temple assistants called Levites, and gatekeepers in rotating shifts as David had planned. Verse 16 then says the temple was finished, and some readers take its placement here to mean the writer saw the work as complete only once regular worship was running.

parts.label: Ships to Ophir (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: From ports on the Gulf of Aqaba, Solomon's men sailed with experienced sailors sent by Hiram, whose Phoenician people were famous seafarers, to Ophir, a gold-rich land whose location is still debated. They brought back hundreds of talents of gold, many tons, though First Kings gives a slightly different figure.

think: When you admire a great achievement, how much does it matter to you who did the hard work behind it and whether they had a choice?
